rule: One tutorial artifact per principle. Other artifacts may compare or complicate it. A Keep is a collection choice, not an obligation to fill every hall.

halls.title: Vectors in your hands
halls.principle: Displacement, magnitude and unit direction; addition; signed projection and remainder
halls.lesson: Continue the point class from Lines. Make two points report their separation as a vector, a length and a direction. Begin with those three readings; return to the projection after they make sense.
halls.carry: Keep the distinction between a position and a displacement. In Launch, a vector describes how much position changes each second.
halls.independent_check:
Place the endpoints three metres apart along X and four along Y. Predict a five-metre gap, then check it. Move both together and check again. Finally bring them together: the cylinder disappears and the direction reads zero.

To inspect the projection, temporarily display `r.along_x` and `r.remainder` in the caption. The complete example already calculates both; its first readout shows only gap, length and direction.

halls.title: A beginning, then a flight
halls.lesson: Continue the sphere as a marker. Give it an initial velocity and calculate its position as time passes. Freeze its rigid body and turn collision off so this first flight follows the calculation alone.
halls.carry: You have calculated where the point should be. Next, let the physics engine keep its velocity while you supply a push.
halls.independent_check:
Keep the upward component at 4 m/s. Double the horizontal component from 3 to 6 m/s. Predict what changes before running: the return still takes 0.8 seconds, while horizontal range grows from 2.4 to 4.8 metres.

Back in the hall, try PAIR. Two complementary launch angles at the same speed can reach the same distance in different times.
halls.selection_note: The selected Bubble Blaster carries the launch velocity in the hand. Compare the existing Launch Arc with a projectile catapult and a human catapult. The enlarged fountain runs ballistic trajectories and pauses its own clock near the apex; the museum continues running.

halls.title: The push ends. Motion stays.
halls.lesson: Use three instances of the familiar point. Give each the same force for the same time and vary only mass. The supplied `free_point.gd` lets them move freely, with gravity and damping set to zero.
halls.carry: A push can end while its consequence continues. Next, choose the push from where the point is now.
halls.independent_check:
Keep the complete example above as your working reference. In a separate script extending `study.gd`, make two points: 1 kg and 2 kg. One button begins both pushes. Apply the same 1 N force to the first for one second and the second for two seconds. Keep an independent remaining-time value for each point. A two-entry array and the loop pattern above are enough. Reading `remaining[i]` gets that point’s clock; assigning `remaining[i] = ...` replaces the entry. Update each clock separately, keeping its index paired with the same point.

Before running, predict their speeds after one second and after both pushes have finished. Also predict whether equal final speed puts them at the same distance from their starting places. Show both speeds and distances from the starting positions in the caption. Keep each starting position before the run; the length of `point.position - start_position` measures distance from it in these straight, forward paths. This reuses the displacement from Lines. Keep one snapshot of both distances when both push clocks first reach zero; the spheres will keep moving while you read it. A boolean flag can record that the snapshot has been taken, and the next button press can clear that flag. Allow for a small difference from the ideal values at the physics-step boundary. Use a clear bay, no gravity or damping, and separate the points so they cannot collide during this comparison.

Check your result by waiting after both clocks reach zero: both points should retain their final velocities until another influence intervenes. Explain which instructions end the push and which settings permit the coasting. Then choose another mass and work out a duration that would give the same final speed. Your code and your prediction are both part of the exercise.
halls.selection_note: The mower turns a 20 × 28 m lawn into a flower trail. Push its held pink handle forward; lateral hand displacement steers with yaw drag. A 14 kg rigid body responds to a bounded model force and rolling resistance. The handle reads model force, drag, distance and signed work; it does not measure muscle force.

halls.title: The room gives a direction
halls.principle: Sample a field; retain a moving state
halls.lesson: Keep the moving point. Replace the fixed push with `sample()`, a function that reads its position and returns an acceleration. Combine an inward pull with a sideways turn.
halls.carry: This force reads position. The next one reads how fast, and in which direction, the point is moving.
halls.independent_check: Change the point’s mass to 4 kg. With the same start and no contact, predict the same path: the requested force grows with mass. Restart, then set the sideways coefficient from 2.8 to zero. Watch what remains of the motion.
halls.selection_note: The upgraded Wind Room drives rigid cubes and familiar points with relative-velocity drag. Aim a held rose point to steer the air, or use the controls at the entry. Walk through the same field. Compare the older Force Vortex, which prescribes a spiral velocity and ejects the visitor, with the primary vortex that integrates acceleration.

halls.title: What resists the journey
halls.principle: Speed-dependent drag, buoyancy approximation and contact friction
halls.lesson: Keep the sphere and enable gravity. Add resistance while its centre lies between heights zero and two metres. The small study uses a height test; it does not build a liquid surface.
halls.carry: Drag resists motion. A spring adds a reason to move back toward an attachment.
halls.independent_check: Increase `coefficient` from 0.6 to 3.0 and restart. At the same speed the drag is five times stronger, until capped. Compare the falling speeds over the available drop; the short fall may end before either reaches a steady speed.
halls.selection_note: Viscosity Layers returns the drag comparison at bench scale. The centrifuge adds a circular hand ride: hold the rose handle, travel around the ring, release into the tangent. It prescribes the circular motion; it does not simulate a physical hinge or rotate the tracked head.

halls.title: A force toward home
halls.principle: Restoring force, coupling, damping and constraints
halls.lesson: Make one spring from the familiar point and a fixed anchor. In your small study, grab the point itself to set its position, then release it to see the spring act. The thin cylinder shows the attachment.
halls.carry: Here a repeating movement comes from forces changing velocity. Next, make a similar repetition by assigning positions.
halls.independent_check: Release from the same position with damping at 0.5, then at 3.0. Predict which will keep moving longer. Restore damping and double stiffness. Compare the stronger return without changing rest length.
halls.selection_note: Compare the physical 6DOF SpringSuspension joint, now pulled with a rose hand grip, with Spring Tower, whose cosine animation illustrates a period. The existing coupled PointBody springs remain the tutorial object.

halls.title: The next body arrives
halls.lesson: Use two sphere points as the tips of two arms. Give each an angle and a turning rate. OFFSET changes one angle once; DRIFT changes how quickly that angle advances.
halls.carry: A circular path can be prescribed. Next, let two points attract each other and see what path results.
halls.independent_check: Press OFFSET with equal rates and watch the 45° gap persist. Restart, press DRIFT and wait thirty seconds: predict an added gap of 72°. Change the rate difference to 2% and predict 36°.

halls.title: The source can move too
halls.lesson: Return to two physical points. Give them opposite starting velocities. Calculate the attraction between them once, apply it to one body, and apply its negative to the other.
halls.carry: These points attract while passing through each other. Bring back collision to ask what lets one body support another.
halls.independent_check: Double only `a.mass` and keep the starting velocities. Predict both responses: the shared force doubles; a’s acceleration stays the same because its mass also doubled; b’s acceleration doubles. Restart to compare.
halls.selection_note: Orbit Walk is a prescribed two-body barycentre diagram. It is a controlled comparison beside the primary mutually attracting points, whose trajectories are integrated.

halls.title: What holds the body up
halls.principle: Support, contact and centre of mass
halls.lesson: Bring back the cube from Primitives. Start with one box resting on one support. Move the support sideways and let the physics engine determine what happens to the load.
halls.carry: Contact can hold a body still. Next, let contact pass motion from one body to another.
halls.independent_check: Change the support’s movement from 1.5 m to 0.1 m and restart. Predict that enough overlap will remain to support the centred cube. Then restore the larger movement. Keep the dimensions and gravity the same.

halls.title: One push reaches another body
halls.lesson: Use the same point twice: one striker and one target. Give the striker one impulse, then let their collision unfold. Start without gravity or a floor so the first question is the impact.
halls.carry: An impulse happens once. In the last hall, hold a trigger to keep adding acceleration to your own movement.
halls.independent_check: Double the striker’s mass while keeping the impulse. Predict its initial speed, then observe the collision separately. Restart each trial. A prediction about the launch speed does not yet tell you how the whole collision will end.
halls.selection_note: Compare two presentations: Momentum Cradle shows ideal input/output poses; Newton's Cradle integrates pendulum angles with an idealized equal-mass collision exchange. Neither is the Jolt collision solver used by bowling. The oversized impact club is beside the bowling ball. A seven-kilogram punching bag beside recoil adds contact and constrained return; both are supporting play, with the bowling sphere still carrying the tutorial.

halls.title: Carry the point through
halls.lesson: Extend the familiar point into a thruster. While held and activated, it reports an acceleration in the direction of your hand. The small station script creates two of these points.
halls.carry: The point now gives you a capacity in the world. Direction, acceleration, resistance and contact are things you can use together. The racer and the larger experiments give you places to try.
halls.independent_check: Aim one hand up and one down. Before pressing, predict that the two thrusts cancel while gravity still acts. Then aim both upward: their 22 m/s² request exceeds the court’s 9.8 m/s² gravity. Release the triggers and watch how velocity continues to change.

archived_halls.title: Two moves, one arrival
archived_halls.lesson: Keep the same point class and introduce a second displacement in the same frame. Place their arrows head to tail and build one result point from a+b. Compare the sum with the two travelled segments. The drafting board and walk-in construction let the same operation be read at two other scales.
archived_halls.carry: A sum can preserve an endpoint without preserving the journey.
archived_halls.independent_check: Choose cancelling displacements, then swap two unequal ones. Show the same arrival and a different intermediate position.

archived_halls.title: What the rail keeps
archived_halls.lesson: Continue with the held point. Project its displacement onto a fixed unit rail and retain the perpendicular remainder. Add the two parts to recover the original. The alignment and crank instruments are nearby comparisons: an alignment score, a component and a turning relation are different quantities. This lesson reconstructs only the projection point.
archived_halls.carry: A selected component does not erase what the operation leaves over.
archived_halls.independent_check: Move the point perpendicular to the rail; verify that the projection stays still while the remainder changes.

vector_compaction: Three vector readings in one hall. Older comparison machines stay in the collection, outside this route.
force_play: Eighteen larger hand-led studies added to the existing eleven-hall route; one tutorial anchor per principle, comparisons remain optional.
